newsitem.title: USA: CORN--U.S. farmers to keep firm grip on new crop.
newsitem.headline: CORN--U.S. farmers to keep firm grip on new crop.

text.p: This year's U.S. corn harvest may not offer immediate relief to end-users pinched by tight stocks as farmers opt to store new crop grain in hopes of higher prices, analysts and merchandisers said.
"We can have a nine-billion-bushel crop but it's not going to get into the channels," said Joe Miller, market analyst at the Indiana Farm Bureau.
"I have not talked to a farmer yet who said he would sell his corn for $3.00," he added. "If this stuff goes into the (storage) bin you're going to have to pay to get it out."

On average, farmers sell seven to eight percent of new crop corn in September and 10 to 17 percent in October, said Don Roose, president of U.S. Commodities, an Iowa-based grain marketing and merchandising firm. "This year we're probably one-third behind (normal levels) nationally," he said.
With current futures prices at the Chicago Board of Trade down more than $2.00 from July's record high of $5.54-1/2 per bushel, farmers had little incentive to sell, Miller noted.
Corn for delivery against CBOT December futures closed up 3/4 cent at $3.14-1/4 a bushel Friday.
Some producers were concerned about crop conditions after below-normal summer temperatures and the threat of an early frost put late-planted plants in jeopardy.

And with abundant, inexpensive grain storage space available and enough money in the bank to last a few months, farmers were unlikely to sell as much new crop corn as they would in a typical year, said Dave Armstrong, analyst with The Chicago Corporation.
"Farmers are in pretty good financial shape, they can stand to wait," he said.

This year's tight stocks forced end-users to buy virtually every kernel of old crop corn, leaving elevator storage bins empty. In addition, U.S. agriculture policy brought an end to government grain storage which freed up even more room.
A Nebraska merchandiser said his elevator's bins were empty for the first time in 16 years. An Illinois dealer said he had never seen empty bins before this year.
"We're probably 8 million bushels behind normal," the Illinios dealer said, referring to typical grain purchases for this time of year.

In anticipation of tight new crop supplies, some end-users have turned to the futures markets in hopes of securing the grain at a lower price, Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) data indicate.
As of Sept. 10, the CFTC Commitment of Traders report showed commercials held long positions in corn of 776 million bushels and were short 636 million bushels.
"The commercial typically this time of year is short," Roose said. "The commercial is long (this year) because he is still covering his end-usage until new crop comes in."
But below normal summer temperatures have slowed crop development and delayed harvest, meaning commercials will have to wait longer than normal for new crop supplies.
